title: Teach Microduck to score a goal
text: What you will build  The final scene contains one Microduck, one football, and one goal. The robot must find the ball, locate the goal, approach a useful kicking position, make contact, and recover its stance. You will learn what each part of this system does and how the parts work together.    1 Understand the mechanism   2 Control and train   3 See and navigate   4 Score autonomously     By the end, you can   Explain how joints, actuators, observations, actions, and rewards relate.  Launch a Newton / Isaac Lab simulation and inspect a fixed policy in action.  Run a bounded training exercise, locate checkpoints, and interpret training curves.  Connect camera detections, ToF ranges, and body attitude to autonomous task states.  Record both successes and failures, distinguishing model metrics from task metrics.     Course route      Chapter  Task      Chapter 1  Meet Microduck: play football first    Chapter 2  Mechanism and control timing    Chapter 3  Learning to walk    Chapter 4  Adapt walking to slopes    Chapter 5  Explore community movement skills    Chapter 6  Design the autonomous football pipeline    Chapter 7  Complete the autonomous task    Chapter 8  Recap and a harder football challenge

title: How to take this course
text: Choose a learning path      Path  What you do  What you need      Observe  Read, inspect the 3D assembly, watch demonstrations, and answer checks.  A modern browser    Use fixed models (recommended)  Copy terminal commands, run simulation, and record observations.  A prepared GPU environment    Practice training  Add your own training, export, and evaluation.  Additional runtime and disk space      For a first pass, complete the fixed-model path, then return to Chapters 3, 4 and 7 for training. Without a GPU, follow the reading path in order. The interactive model and examples do not launch Isaac.    Prerequisites   Open a Linux terminal, change directories, and copy multiline commands.  Read basic Python functions, arrays, and parameters. Prior PPO knowledge is not required.  Understand positions, angles, and velocities; robot coordinate frames are introduced in the course.    About your training results  Your checkpoint is a practice artifact. Later chapters explicitly use the course models in  models/ ; they never select the latest training run automatically. Using your own policy requires an explicit checkpoint and a new evaluation.     A useful lab routine   Read the expected result before running a command.  Run commands from the repository root. Use a new output directory for every run.  Keep the command, seed, and result—including failures.  Answer the chapter check before moving on.   Reading and exercise durations are planning estimates, not training-time guarantees. The first launch may download assets, compile kernels, and populate rendering caches.

title: Prepare your environment
text:
Runtime requirements  The reference environment is Ubuntu 24.04 on DGX Spark (aarch64), Python 3.12, Isaac Sim 6, and pinned Isaac Lab / Newton revisions. Simulation uses Newton’s native actuator path. Other GPUs or versions may run, but the course results do not automatically apply to them.  You need an NVIDIA driver, a GPU-enabled graphical desktop, Git, Docker, and network access to NVIDIA package sources. None of these are required for reading the website. Review the Isaac Sim license before installing the simulator.    Download the course and models    Terminal · Bash  Copy command    mkdir -p "$HOME/microduck"
cd "$HOME/microduck"
git clone https://github.com/NV-DLI/Microduck-Workshop.git
cd Microduck-Workshop
python3 scripts/workshop.py verify-models    The models are included in the repository, so no Hugging Face login is required. The verification command checks every model’s SHA-256. Continue only when all files match. Course weights and student outputs are stored separately.    Workspace    Microduck-Workshop/
├── web/          # HTML course
├── lab/          # simulation and learning code
├── models/       # fixed course models
├── scripts/      # lab entry points
└── outputs/      # your runs (created when needed)      Prepare the simulator  First prepare system tools. The commands below install Git, Python virtual-environment support, and video encoding. Set up Docker using its  Ubuntu instructions ;  docker info  should show server information without a permission error.    Terminal · Bash  Copy command    sudo apt-get update
sudo apt-get install -y git python3-venv ffmpeg
docker info
export UV_HTTP_TIMEOUT=600      Terminal · Bash  Copy command    python3 scripts/workshop.py setup
python3 scripts/workshop.py doctor     setup  prepares the pinned runtime. If you already have a matching Isaac Lab checkout, bind it using  --isaaclab /path/to/IsaacLab .  doctor  checks Python, models, GPU, the desktop display setting, and navigation dependencies. Resolve failed checks before continuing.   Launch from your desktop terminal  Run GUI commands in a terminal on the GPU machine’s desktop. The website provides lessons and commands; Isaac opens in its own window. On the first launch, allow shaders and assets to finish loading.     Before you continue    Terminal · Bash  Copy command    python3 scripts/workshop.py inspect-model --model models/walk.onnx    Expected result: input and output names, tensor shapes, and model identity. If the GPU is unavailable, use the troubleshooting page before proceeding. Keep the pinned physics backend and model combination.

title: Meet Microduck: play football first
text:
A small robot that learns new skills  Microduck is an open biped from Pollen Robotics and Hugging Face with 14 actuated joints. Start with the official walking and right-foot kick ONNX policies in Isaac Sim, then learn how Isaac Lab trains and evaluates new skills.    Open the pitch and try the keyboard  Complete  setup  and run this from the repository root. Click the Isaac Sim window to focus it. The robot, ball and goal use the same dimensions and physical settings as the autonomous task. Use an English keyboard input mode so an IME does not consume movement keys.      Walk toward the ball, stop, then switch to the right-foot kick.     Terminal  Copy command    python3 scripts/workshop.py manual \
  --seconds 600 \
  --output outputs/manual-football-01        Key  Action      W / S  Forward / backward    A / D  Step left / right    Q / E  Turn left / right    Release movement keys  Stand with zero velocity command    Space  Right-foot kick, then stand    R / Esc  Restart / exit      Walk toward the ball, stop with the ball in front of the right foot, and face the goal before pressing Space. Reposition after a miss; press R after a fall. You choose the target and direction; the policies coordinate the joints.    How Isaac Sim builds the experiment   Scroll horizontally to view the full diagram    Scene to motion  USD scene：Robot, pitch, ball and goal；Physics：Mass, contact and motors；Policy and input：Keys → ONNX → joint goals       Scene to motion     USD scene  Robot, pitch, ball and  goal   Physics  Mass, contact and motors   Policy and input  Keys → ONNX → joint goals    Rendering, physics and policy have separate roles. A different skill reuses the scene; a different ball position reuses the walking actor.   The robot USD includes joints, collision geometry and inertial properties. The ball has a 3.5 cm radius and 45 g mass; the goal opening is 38.8 cm wide. Isaac Sim provides the scene and rendering; Isaac Lab configures the Newton physics backend.    Python · 核心代码节选  Full source ↗    cfg.scene.ball = RigidObjectCfg(
    prim_path="{ENV_REGEX_NS}/Ball",
    spawn=sim_utils.SphereCfg(
        radius=0.035,
        mass_props=sim_utils.MassPropertiesCfg(mass=0.045),
        collision_props=sim_utils.CollisionPropertiesCfg(),
        rigid_props=UsdPhysicsRigidBodyCfg(rigid_body_enabled=True),
    ),
    init_state=RigidObjectCfg.InitialStateCfg(pos=(0.0, 0.0, 0.035)),
)      Fix the scene and hardware contract  The indoor scene uses a 1 × 1.6 m mat, a secured steel-mesh goal measuring 40 cm wide × 20 cm deep × 25 cm high, and a 7 cm diameter, 45 g ball. This supports short approaches and shots, not arbitrary obstacle avoidance in a confined space. With an assumed 6 mm frame diameter, post centres are 39.4 cm apart and the clear opening is 38.8 × 24.4 cm. Localization uses centre spacing; scoring uses the clear opening.  The four mat patterns share dimensions, robot, lighting and contact model. Frame and mesh have collision geometry. The mat uses a flush rigid contact plane; curled edges, compression and an unsecured goal are not modeled. Wire thickness, friction and material response remain assumptions to measure on the actual products. Visual detail alone does not establish physical accuracy.      Mat patterns A–D at identical dimensions and physical state. These illustrations isolate appearance; they are not four task outcomes.   The robot uses official Microduck CAD with backlash and full-body collisions. The course pins the XL330 BAM actuator fit, 200 Hz physics and 50 Hz actor updates. The walking actor controls 14 of the 15 physical servos; it does not independently drive the mouth. Full-body collision geometry allows the head, legs and battery to rest on the ground after a fall.  This is a versioned simulation configuration. The camera corresponds to GC2093, but simulation samples at 960 × 540 and 15 Hz with an uncalibrated 70° horizontal field of view. ToF and body IMU models also contain approximations. This does not establish parity with every latest firmware or hardware error, nor validate full deployment on RK3566. Check the real hardware revision, voltage, joint offsets, lens parameters and end-to-end delay before transfer.  Comparison with upstream on 23 October 2026 found no changes to the pinned CAD meshes, base mass/joint parameters or motor fit. This scene adds the official full-body contact configuration. The mechanical viewer retains the Pi Zero 2 W board mesh in the CAD, while current Beta software targets RK3566. The displayed board is not evidence of the latest electronics.    How two small policies control the body      File  Size  Role      walk.onnx  793,705 bytes, about 0.79 MB  Walking and standing    kick-teacher.onnx  793,685 bytes, about 0.79 MB  Right-foot kick      Both actors map 61 observations to 14 joint actions through hidden layers of 512, 256 and 128 units with ELU activations. Their input normalization is embedded in ONNX. Keyboard commands set velocity, not individual joint angles. A bounded kick blends back to standing; this lab does not load the course residual actor.                                                                                                         Observation  61       ⋮  Normalize  Hidden 1  512       ⋮  ELU  Hidden 2  256       ⋮  ELU  Hidden 3  128       ⋮  ELU  Action  14       ⋮  Joint actions  Fully connected · inference every 20 ms · no camera images    Circles show a subset of units; numbers give actual dimensions. The official walking and kick actors share this structure but have different weights. The training critic is not shown.     Python · 核心代码节选  Full source ↗    # Read the state once per policy step, then select the active skill.
obs = env.observation_manager.compute(update_history=True)["policy"]
action = walk(obs)

if kick_start is not None:
    phase = (step - kick_start) * 0.02
    weight = 1.0 if phase < 0.14 else max(0.0, 1.0 - (phase - 0.14) / 0.12)
    if weight:
        action = torch.lerp(action, kick(obs), weight)

# The action manager maps network outputs to joint targets.
env.action_manager.process_action(action)    The lab holds the kick for 0.14 s and blends back over 0.12 s. This is a handoff setting, not retraining of the official weights. Small policy files do not imply a small simulator memory footprint.    Terminal  Copy command    python3 scripts/workshop.py inspect-model --model models/walk.onnx      Who decided the next step?   Check your understanding  Which decisions did you make for the robot?   Show explanation  You identified the ball and goal, estimated distance, selected a route and stance, and decided when to kick. Chapters 6 and 7 automate those decisions.    Next, inspect the mechanism and the timing between policy and physics.

title: Mechanism and control timing
text: From assembly to components  Microduck is a small biped. Its legs support and move the body, the neck directs its view, and the trunk houses computing, power, and connections. Visual meshes describe appearance. Joints and collision geometry describe permitted motion and contact. These play different roles in simulation.       Open interactive model    Assembled   Exploded  Reset view    Click a part or its label to inspect it  Left-drag to orbit, middle-drag to pan, scroll or pinch to zoom. Use the slider to separate the parts.    Move the separation slider to inspect the leg and head servos. Click their labels to identify the driven joints, then inspect the camera, controller board and battery. Reset to trace the leg joints.   Hardware revision and simulation joints  There are 15 servos: five per leg, four for the head and neck, and one for the beak. The policy drives 14 joints; the beak remains fixed. The CAD retains a Raspberry Pi Zero 2 W board mesh; this is not the current Beta RK3566 electronics configuration. Chapter 6 introduces the simulated sensors.     Parts, joints, and degrees of freedom  A pen held at its tip can rotate in several directions, while a hinge normally rotates around one fixed axis. Robot joints impose similar constraints. A degree of freedom is an independent variable needed to describe permitted motion; a component count describes physical pieces. The 70 components in this viewer do not imply 70 policy actions.      Region  Active joints  Main role      Each leg  Hip yaw, roll, pitch; knee; ankle: 5 joints  Support the body and place the foot    Neck and head  Neck pitch; head pitch, yaw, roll: 4 joints  Orient the camera and head    Beak  Physical servo; not controlled by this policy  Shown in 3D model, excluded from the 14-action interface      Select a hip servo and inspect its output shaft and nearby bearing. The servo controls an active angle, the bearing supports rotation, and brackets connect adjacent joints. Material, shape, and assembly clearance affect motion. The viewer preserves 3D model detail but does not simulate screw preload, plastic elasticity, or cable forces; it is an anatomy aid rather than manufacturing documentation.    How software moves the mechanism    1 Policy action   2 Joint targets   3 Actuator torque   4 Physics update   5 New observation   A policy does not teleport the robot to a desired position. It outputs actions that become joint targets. Actuators produce torque based on the difference between target and measured state. The resulting motion depends on contact, gravity, inertia, and friction.  The policy runs at 50 Hz and physics at 200 Hz: each action spans four physics steps. Backlash introduces passive joints representing transmission play. Passive joints are not additional policy outputs.    Describe motion with frames      Frame  What is expressed here      World  Pitch, goal, and overall robot position    Body  Forward, lateral, and turn commands; ball relative to the robot    Camera  Image rays and detected target directions    Joint-local  A joint’s axis and angle       Check your understanding  If the head joints stay fixed, is the camera image necessarily stable?   Show explanation  No. Body pitch and roll move the neck and camera. Image stability depends on camera orientation relative to the world, not only on joint angles.      Exercise: trace one load path  Start with the assembled model. Trace a path from the left foot through the ankle, shin, knee, thigh, and hip. Ground support reaches the body through this chain. Explode the assembly and select the servos and brackets around a joint. Identify the fixed housing and the part driven by its output. Explosion offsets are display positions, not physically reachable joint poses.  A servo combines a motor, reduction gears, position feedback, and control electronics. Reaching a target takes time and is limited by torque, speed, friction, and backlash. A policy issuing an angle does not mean the joint instantly reaches it. Chapter 2 observes this difference; Chapter 3 explains how a policy learns around it.   Check your understanding  Does moving the foot farther out in the exploded view change the simulated leg length?   Show explanation  No. The web view explains components. Robot description files define simulated dimensions and joint connections.      What the policy receives and produces  Chapter 1 runs inference with a trained policy. It maps the current observation to 14 joint actions without updating neural-network parameters. Changing the velocity command tests the same model under a different request; it is not training. Choosing a different model file changes the policy.      Observation, in interface order  Width  What it tells the policy      Angular velocity and projected gravity  6  Body rotation and tilt    Relative joint positions  14  Pose relative to the nominal posture    Joint velocities  14  Motion at each joint    Previous action  14  Previous control output and temporal context    Velocity, head, and body commands  3 + 4 + 6  Requested behavior                                                                                                             Observation  61       ⋮  Normalize  Hidden 1  512       ⋮  ELU  Hidden 2  256       ⋮  ELU  Hidden 3  128       ⋮  ELU  Action  14       ⋮  Joint actions  Fully connected · inference every 20 ms · no camera images    Circles show a subset of units; numbers give actual dimensions. The official walking and kick actors share this structure but have different weights. The training critic is not shown.   These values total 61. Reordering joints breaks their meaning even if the input still has 61 entries: the policy might read a knee as a hip. Course entry points preserve ordering, nominal posture, and control timing. Begin by changing commands, duration, and output directories; modify observation construction only after understanding the interface.

title: Learning to walk
text:
One reinforcement-learning loop  The policy receives a vector containing body attitude, angular velocity, joint state, a velocity command, and the previous action. It outputs joint actions, physics advances, and rewards measure progress toward the objective. PPO collects a batch of interactions, updates the policy, and samples again.    1 Observe   2 Sample actions   3 Simulate   4 Compute rewards   5 Update PPO   The environment count is the number of simultaneous robot copies. Iterations repeat collection and optimization. More environments increase parallel sampling and memory demand. A rising training reward means the optimized objective is improving; independent behavior checks are still necessary.    Why PPO looks beyond immediate reward  Lifting a foot can briefly reduce stability while being necessary for forward progress. Reinforcement learning therefore considers return over time rather than just the current reward. A discount factor reduces the weight of more distant rewards, balancing immediate feedback with longer-term consequences.  In PPO, the actor chooses actions and the critic estimates future return. An outcome better than the critic expected receives a positive advantage estimate, encouraging a higher probability for the corresponding action; a worse outcome does the opposite. PPO limits how far an update moves from the old policy to reduce abrupt changes. It does not guarantee that every update improves real task success.  A critic may receive additional simulation information to evaluate trajectories, but the deployed actor must depend only on observations available at runtime. A simulator knowing exact body velocity does not imply that hardware has a perfect velocity sensor. Keep training or scoring ground truth out of the deployed controller.  When designing rewards, list desired behaviors and then consider shortcuts. Rewarding ball motion may encourage body collisions; rewarding stillness may discourage walking. Track both goals and constraints: velocity error, episode length, falls, joint limits, and contact type. This chapter practices the training loop; Chapter 7 tests the complete task definition.    Run a short training exercise    Terminal · Bash  Copy command    python3 scripts/workshop.py train-walk \
  --num-envs 64 \
  --iterations 20 \
  --seed 101 \
  --output outputs/student-walk-01    This is a workflow exercise, not a promise that 20 iterations will learn to walk. Expected result: terminal progress, a new run directory, checkpoints, and an exported policy. Observe loss, return, and episode length without committing to a long training run.    Terminal · Bash  Copy command    python3 scripts/workshop.py tensorboard \
  --logdir outputs/student-walk-01 \
  --port 6006    Open the local TensorBoard address printed in the terminal. Compare reward with episode length. If reward grows while episodes remain short, consider whether the objective rewards a brief action followed by a fall.  Current practice uses full-body contacts, including the head and legs during falls. New outputs are separate experiments; historical learning curves retain their original configuration. Training does not render frames; policy playback uses the shared RTX lighting and materials.    From a smoke run to a longer training run  The 20-iteration exercise checks the pipeline, not convergence. A longer run below uses 1024 environments for 2500 iterations in a new output directory. Judge convergence with curves and independent evaluation, not iteration count alone.    Terminal  Copy command    python3 scripts/workshop.py train-walk \
  --num-envs 1024 --iterations 2500 --seed 101 \
  --output outputs/walking-training-01    Use TensorBoard to compare reward, episode length, falls and velocity error. Use the short-run export in the next section, or explicitly select outputs/walking-training-01/exported/policy.onnx after this longer run. Neither changes the official model.    Explicitly test your own policy    Terminal · Bash  Copy command    python3 scripts/workshop.py walk \
  --model outputs/student-walk-01/exported/policy.onnx \
  --velocity 0.30 0.00 0.00 \
  --seconds 12 \
  --seed 202 \
  --output outputs/student-walk-test-01    Here you deliberately select your own model. Compare support, drift, and falls with the official model from Chapter 1. Later lessons still use  models/walk.onnx ; this export does not change their default.   Go further  To increase the budget, choose a new output directory and try, for example, 1,024 environments and 500 iterations. Check available memory and time first. A saved checkpoint is not a qualification result. Evaluate unseen seeds and retain failures.     Terminal  Copy command    python3 scripts/workshop.py walk \
  --model models/walk.onnx --velocity 0.3 0 0 \
  --seconds 12 --seed 202 \
  --output outputs/official-walk-comparison-01    Match command, duration and seed. Compare falls, distance and actual velocity, then test standing at zero command. One moving demonstration is not a complete skill benchmark.    Why domain randomization matters  Real actuators do not have identical friction, delay, and backlash on every run. Varying parameters in training exposes the policy to more conditions. A narrow range can overfit; an excessively broad range can make learning difficult. Randomization can improve robustness but does not replace hardware testing.   Check your understanding  Why is the highest-reward training episode not an independent test?   Show explanation  It contributed to learning or selection, and reward may differ from task success. Independent testing uses predetermined scenarios and success criteria and counts every outcome.      Checkpoints, curves, and independent tests  Practice starts from random parameters rather than the course walking weights. Each PPO iteration gathers trajectories from several environments and then updates the policy. Rewards combine velocity tracking, body attitude, action smoothness, and contact-related terms. Two policies with similar total rewards may obtain them through accurate motion or simply moving less; inspect both behavior and individual reward terms.   initial.pt  records initialization;  model_*.pt  files are checkpoints;  env.yaml  and  agent.yaml  preserve environment and optimizer settings;  exported/policy.onnx  is the inference export. A checkpoint can contain optimizer state, while ONNX normally preserves the inference graph. They are not interchangeable file formats.  Record the training budget, held-out test seeds, and observed behavior. The 20-iteration exercise teaches sampling, updates, saving, and export. A weak practice policy is no reason to replace downstream course defaults. For a larger budget, keep the earlier run, use a new output directory, and state whether you changed environment count, iteration count, or rewards.   Check your understanding  Does saving only ONNX guarantee an exact training continuation?   Show explanation  No. Exact continuation also needs optimizer, normalization and random states, together with matching configuration. Preserve full checkpoints and training settings.      Will a flat-ground skill handle a slope?  You can now collect rollouts, update PPO, export ONNX and test a policy. Will its foot clearance and balance adjustments work on a slope? Predict the outcome, then test the same policy in Chapter 4.

title: Adapt walking to slopes
text:
Start with a testable question  Do not assume the old actor will fail. Hold the policy, command, duration, friction and initial-state distribution fixed while varying slope. Test traversal and balance, not just a single attractive frame.   Scroll horizontally to view the full diagram    Terrain generalization  Baseline：Same actor: flat/up/down；Isaac Lab training：Sample parallel terrains；Held-out evaluation：Arrival, falls, speed error       Terrain generalization     Baseline  Same actor: flat/up/down   Isaac Lab training  Sample parallel terrains   Held-out evaluation  Arrival, falls, speed  error    Evaluate before adapting. Retain flat-ground ability while testing improvements on slopes.     Build a flat–ramp–landing scene  The surface has a 0.35 m flat approach, a 1 m horizontal ramp, and a landing. Positive angles ascend; negative angles descend. A continuous collision mesh avoids unintended steps. Visual materials do not determine contact dynamics.      The darker surface marks the ramp; gold guides show direction and green marks the target. These visual markings do not change contact physics.              Flat: 0.35 m  Ramp run: 1 m  Landing      h(x) = tan(α) · clip(x − 0.35, 0, 1)    Slope α / °       Adjust the slope to compare ascent and descent. Horizontal and vertical scales match; the landing height changes with the angle.    坡面高度  \[h(x)=\tan(\alpha)\,\operatorname{clip}(x-0.35,0,1)\]     Python · 核心代码节选  Full source ↗    slope = math.tan(math.radians(cfg.slope_deg))
xs = [0.0, 2.35, 3.35, 6.0]
zs = [0.0, 0.0, slope, slope]
vertices = [(x, y, z) for x, z in zip(xs, zs) for y in [0.0, 4.0]]    The mesh uses offset local coordinates; the robot spawn corresponds to x = 0 in the equation. Isaac Lab TerrainGenerator and TerrainImporter reuse this geometry for visualization, physics and parallel tasks.    Test the official walking policy first    Terminal  Copy command    python3 scripts/workshop.py terrain \
  --model models/walk.onnx \
  --slope 5 --num-envs 1 --seconds 20 --seed 42001 \
  --output outputs/slope-up-05    Without --headless this opens Isaac Sim. Use --num-envs 5 --headless for batched evaluation, and test 0, ±5, ±10 and ±15 degrees in separate output directories. The first 2 s are standing; then the command is 0.25 m/s. Actual speed may differ.  Success requires reaching x ≥ 1.45 m within 20 s with lateral error below 0.3 m and staying upright throughout. A fall remains a failure even if the body later slides across the finish. Reports separate reaching, falls and velocity RMSE.      Slope  Pass  Fall      0°  5/5  0/5    +5°  0/5  0/5    -5°  0/5  5/5    +10°  0/5  0/5    -10°  0/5  5/5    +15°  0/5  0/5    -15°  0/5  5/5      Each angle uses five lightly perturbed starts. Flat trials pass; uphill trials stall without falling; downhill trials fall. This small baseline identifies an adaptation need, not general reliability.    Why flat-ground experience may not transfer  A slope changes foot clearance, gravity along the surface and usable friction. Insufficient clearance or propulsion can stall ascent; downhill landing and balance changes can cause falls. Survival alone misses stalled traversal.    Continue learning across terrain types  Keep the official ONNX unchanged. Initialize a new actor from its weights and normalization, with a fresh critic and optimizer. Mix 25% flat terrain with ascending and descending terrain. Verify initial actor parity before learning.    Terminal  Copy command    python3 scripts/workshop.py train-terrain \
  --model models/walk.onnx \
  --num-envs 256 --iterations 1000 --seed 43001 \
  --output outputs/terrain-training-01    Training slopes are tan(α), not degrees: 0.03–0.22 is about 1.7°–12.4°. Training uses pyramidal and inverted slopes; evaluation uses straight ramps and separate seeds.    Python · 核心代码节选  Full source ↗    sub_terrains = {
    "flat": MeshPlaneTerrainCfg(proportion=0.25),
    "slopes": HfPyramidSlopedTerrainCfg(
        proportion=0.375, slope_range=(0.03, 0.22), platform_width=0.7
    ),
    "descending": HfInvertedPyramidSlopedTerrainCfg(
        proportion=0.375, slope_range=(0.03, 0.22), platform_width=0.7
    ),
}    The fixed terrain weights retain their original training lineage. Current practice runs use the same full-contact robot as the demonstrations, so their contact configuration differs from the historical training and defines a new experiment. Training is physics-only; inspect exported policies in the shared RTX scene.    Balance and direction both matter   第一步：定义有物理含义的误差  \[e_{\omega}=\omega_z-\omega_z^*,\qquad u=\frac{e_{\omega}}{\sigma}\]    第二步：把误差转换为平滑、有界的奖励  \[r_{\omega}=\exp(-u^2)=\exp\!\left[-\left(\frac{\omega_z-\omega_z^*}{0.15}\right)^2\right]\]     Python · 核心代码节选  Full source ↗    def yaw_rate_tracking(env, std=0.15):
    # Match the commanded turn rate without penalizing normal roll/pitch motion.
    velocity = env.scene["robot"].data.root_link_ang_vel_b.torch
    target = env.command_manager.get_command("base_velocity")[:, 2]

    # Squared, normalized error gives a symmetric reward in (0, 1].
    return torch.exp(-((velocity[:, 2] - target) / std).square())


cfg.rewards.yaw_precision = RewardTermCfg(
    func=yaw_rate_tracking, weight=4.0, params={"std": 0.15}
)      Terminal  Copy command    python3 scripts/workshop.py train-terrain \
  --model models/walk.onnx \
  --resume outputs/terrain-training-01/model_999.pt \
  --refine-heading --num-envs 256 --iterations 1500 --seed 43002 \
  --output outputs/terrain-heading-01

python3 scripts/workshop.py train-terrain \
  --model models/walk.onnx \
  --resume outputs/terrain-heading-01/model_2498.pt \
  --refine-heading --yaw-precision \
  --num-envs 256 --iterations 2000 --seed 43003 \
  --output outputs/terrain-direction-01      Compare both actors with the same benchmark      Ascent10°: official actor above, terrain actor below. The original stalls while the adapted actor reaches the target. Matched starts and synchronized simulation time; this illustration does not replace the full benchmark.       Downhill at 10°: the official policy is above and the terrain policy below. The official robot loses balance but remains supported by the continuous ground. The terrain policy stays upright but fails the arrival condition because of lateral drift. Both use the same starting setup and play in synchronized simulation time; the wide view retains motion beyond the ramp. This separate recording seed is excluded from the table below. Staying upright is not the same as completing the task.     Terminal  Copy command    python3 scripts/workshop.py terrain \
  --model models/terrain-walk.onnx \
  --slope 5 --num-envs 5 --seconds 20 --seed 49001 --headless \
  --output outputs/terrain-evaluation-up-05    Use the fixed0.79 MB terrain actor by default. Explicitly select outputs/terrain-direction-01/exported/policy.onnx to test your own export. Chapters1 and7 retain the original walking actor.  Use matched evaluation seeds and angles for both actors. Report flat, uphill and downhill success, falls, tracking error and training time. Stalling is not success, and slope improvements do not justify losing flat-ground ability.      Slope  Official pass  Terrain pass  Terrain falls  Terrain speed RMSE      0°  5/5  5/5  0/5  0.094 m/s    +5°  0/5  5/5  0/5  0.105 m/s    -5°  0/5  5/5  0/5  0.089 m/s    +10°  0/5  5/5  0/5  0.122 m/s    -10°  0/5  2/5  0/5  0.090 m/s    +15°  0/5  0/5  5/5  0.210 m/s    -15°  0/5  0/5  5/5  0.179 m/s      Each angle uses five environments with fixed seed 49001, excluded from model training and selection, and official full-body contacts for both actors. Reusing this seed after correcting the support surface does not create additional independent samples. Success criteria are unchanged. The table averages each environment’s speed RMSE over moving-command samples before its first fall. The lateral gate applies at arrival, not continuously. This small sample does not establish general slope reliability. See the  per-environment results .  The terrain actor passes all five trials on flat ground, ±5° and +10°. At −10° it stays upright in all five but misses the arrival region three times; it falls in every ±15° trial. Stability, direction and completion are distinct metrics. Five trials per angle cannot isolate a parameter effect. Inspect failures before changing training; the shared interface does not qualify this actor for football approach and kick handoff.   Check your understanding  Why evaluate on terrain geometry different from training?   Show explanation  To test transfer to new geometry and initial states. Both actors share evaluation conditions; tuning on those results makes them development data.      What else can this platform teach?  You changed the world with Isaac Sim, adapted a policy in Isaac Lab and tested its scope. Next, explore community jumping and balancing tasks.

title: Explore community movement skills
text: What else can the same robot learn?  Community projects train jumping and ball balancing using different tasks, rewards and initial states. These demonstrations come from their original simulation environments and do not establish equivalent Newton or hardware performance.      Community jump demonstration in the original four-times slow motion. Observe takeoff, flight, landing and the standing handoff.       Community ball-balancing demonstration: watch the moving support surface and continuous posture corrections.       Skill  Observations and actions  Rewards and completion      Jumping  Body state and a jump command → joint actions  Height, landing posture and recovery    Basketball balance  Robot and ball state → joint actions  Balance, relative position and survival    Walking  Body state and velocity command → joint actions  Speed tracking, stability, energy and smoothness      Isaac Sim supplies props and contact geometry; Isaac Lab organizes observations, rewards and reset distributions. Equal observation dimensions do not guarantee compatibility: the jump policy repurposes a command field as a launch trigger.    Define a skill’s boundaries  Walking continuously accepts velocity commands. A kick is a short skill with a start and an end. Integrating it into an autonomous task requires entry conditions, a defined exit state, and a way to stop when conditions are unsafe.      Skill  Observations and actions  Rewards and completion      Jumping  Body state and a jump command → joint actions  Height, landing posture and recovery    Basketball balance  Robot and ball state → joint actions  Balance, relative position and survival    Walking  Body state and velocity command → joint actions  Speed tracking, stability, energy and smoothness        Why ONNX files are not interchangeable  ONNX is a model representation, not a universal robot-skill protocol. The walking model takes 61 inputs, while the kicking residual takes 62. Both output 14 numbers, yet they are not interchangeable. Input ordering, additional state, action scaling, teacher blending, and termination conditions are all part of the runtime contract.  After inspecting the models, record their input and output shapes. Explain why successfully loading a file only proves that its format is readable, not that the robot will perform a skill. A valid file can still receive the wrong units or joint order. The fixed task entry point uses weights together with their required conventions.  Watch the kick in three phases: before it, inspect ball and support-foot positions; during it, identify whether contact comes from the foot or another body part; afterwards, inspect recovery of support. Pause the video in each phase and describe the entry and completion conditions. This is more informative than asking only whether the ball moved.    Describe a skill by its contract  Describe a skill using entry conditions, observations, actions, and exit conditions. A kick requires a useful right-foot ball position, goal alignment, stable support, and fresh target information. Execution combines the kicking teacher with a residual correction. It must then return to a stable standing or walking state; touching the ball alone does not finish the task.  A residual adds a constrained correction to an existing action. This reduces what must be learned from scratch but inherits the teacher’s operating range. Starting a local kick far from the ball does not make it search or approach. Navigation creates a valid handoff state; the skill performs its local action.   Check your understanding  The robot is beside the ball, but its remembered position has expired. Should the kick start immediately?   Show explanation  No. Observe again and confirm the entry conditions. Proximity alone does not guarantee valid inputs.      Executing a skill is not completing a task  These policies already use joint and IMU feedback for balance. They do not yet decide where the football is, which route to take or when to kick. The next chapter designs that external-perception and planning chain.

title: Design the autonomous football pipeline
text: Turn manual decisions into a system   Scroll horizontally to view the full diagram    Autonomous football data flow  Sensors：RGB / ToF / IMU / joints；Detection：Image → ball / goal；Geometry：Pixels and pose → location；Kick stance：Goal direction → pose；Approach：Nav2 path → body velocity；Motion and checks：Walk / kick → observation        Isaac Sim: acquire and interpret sensor data   Planning and execution: goals become actions        Sensors  RGB / ToF / IMU / joints   Detection  Image → ball / goal   Geometry  Pixels and pose → location   Kick stance  Goal direction → pose   Approach  Nav2 path → body velocity   Motion and checks  Walk / kick → observation    At every stage, identify the data source, coordinate frame, freshness and recovery behavior.       Stage  Input  Method or model  Output      Detection  Isaac Sim RGB images  Object detector  Ball/goal boxes, classes and confidence    Target localization  Pixels, intrinsics, head joints and posture  Geometry and object-size constraints  Timestamped relative target positions    Range and posture  VL53L8CX 8×8 ToF and IMU  Validity checks and orientation estimation  Range sectors, posture and valid flags    Kick stance  Ball, goal direction and kick offset  Geometry; no new neural network  Target position and heading    Route and approach  Map, current pose and target stance  Nav2 Navfn and approach controller  Path and body velocity commands    Motion skills  Body state and velocity/kick command  Walking ONNX, kick teacher and residual  14 joint targets    Coordination  Stage outputs and timestamps  State machine and readiness checks  Walk, re-observe, kick or stop      Not every stage needs a learned model. Detection and motion use networks; geometry, path planning and task transitions can use explicit algorithms. Isaac Sim connects the scene and sensors; Isaac Lab trains and evaluates motion skills.    Three complementary sources      Stage  Input  Method or model  Output      Detection  Isaac Sim RGB images  Object detector  Ball/goal boxes, classes and confidence    Target localization  Pixels, intrinsics, head joints and posture  Geometry and object-size constraints  Timestamped relative target positions    Range and posture  VL53L8CX 8×8 ToF and IMU  Validity checks and orientation estimation  Range sectors, posture and valid flags    Kick stance  Ball, goal direction and kick offset  Geometry; no new neural network  Target position and heading    Route and approach  Map, current pose and target stance  Nav2 Navfn and approach controller  Path and body velocity commands    Motion skills  Body state and velocity/kick command  Walking ONNX, kick teacher and residual  14 joint targets    Coordination  Stage outputs and timestamps  State machine and readiness checks  Walk, re-observe, kick or stop      The RGB detector finds image regions resembling a ball. ToF measures ranges across an 8 × 8 forward-facing grid; it is not a 360-degree lidar. A body IMU estimates attitude so image rays and ranges can be interpreted in the right frame. No single sensor supplies the complete world state.  The simulation uses GC2093 camera and VL53L8CX ToF profiles. Images are processed at 960 × 540 and 15 Hz. Lens field of view and noise settings are simulation assumptions; physical devices require calibration.    From a pixel to a spatial ray  Let a detection center be pixel (u, v), with camera focal lengths (fx, fy) and principal point (cx, cy). In a common camera convention, the viewing ray is proportional to ((u−cx)/fx, (v−cy)/fy, 1). This gives direction but cannot distinguish a small nearby object from a larger distant one. Range or a known geometric constraint is still needed.  Camera coordinates commonly use x right, y down, z forward. Here the body convention is x forward, y left, z up. Transform using the camera’s rotation and translation relative to the body rather than mixing same-named axes. Head motion changes this transform, so localization requires joint state at the appropriate time.  An 8 × 8 ToF grid does not provide 64 independent object labels. One cell may cover both floor and ball, and close reflections may be invalid. Check measurement status and range before associating a return with an image target. Treating an invalid reading as an obstacle-free direction gives navigation a false premise.    A past observation can become stale  After moving or tilting its head, the robot may lose the ball from view. Odometry can update a remembered relative position briefly, but error accumulates. Stale observations, invalid ranges, or lost ground constraints require stopping and reobserving. Missing data is not free space.   Check your understanding  If a ball box is accurate, can its center be used directly as a world coordinate?   Show explanation  No. Pixels give an image direction. Spatial position also requires a camera model, camera pose, and distance or geometric constraints.      The ball center is not the destination  Walking straight toward the ball center can cause premature contact or approach from the wrong side. A useful target lies behind the ball. The ball-to-goal direction defines the shooting axis; move backward along it and account for the kicking foot’s lateral offset.   A planar geometry exercise  Direction  d = (goal − ball) / ‖goal − ball‖  Target  target = ball − distance × d + lateral × normal(d)    Expected result: a target position, heading, and a planar diagram. Change the ball’s lateral coordinate and observe how the target moves. This exercise uses known 2D points to teach geometry; autonomous execution uses sensor estimates.    How path planning and walking divide the work  A planner searches for a route through a representation of space. An occupancy grid divides the floor into cells for obstacles, free space, and unknown space. A robot has a footprint: it cannot pass through every gap that admits a mathematical point. Reserving clearance is necessary when turning a geometric route into executable motion.  Nav2 provides CPU navigation services in the full task, while the walking policy maintains bipedal balance. The upper layer requests a target or velocity; the lower layer drives servos. Actuator delay and gait error can move the robot away from its plan, so the system must observe and reconsider instead of assuming exact command execution.  The hand-calculation exercise studies stance geometry only: it does not call Nav2 or place obstacles. The full task uses one robot, ball, and goal in an empty field. Adding obstacles requires new checks for sensor coverage, unknown space, clearance, and collisions. Empty-field results do not establish obstacle-avoidance performance.    Approach in stages    1 Search and observe   2 Coarse approach   3 Fine alignment   4 Check kick conditions   5 Kick and recover   At a distance, reducing range is the main priority. Nearby, motion must become more precise while preserving visibility, heading, and foot placement. Being close enough is not sufficient if heading is wrong.  A planner supplies a route or direction; the walking policy executes it. A valid planned path does not prove the robot has traversed it. The system must handle tracking errors, contact, and sensor updates.      Focus on approach and stance adjustment: control relative position and heading, not just apparent ball size.     Work through a stance target  Subtract the ball position from the goal center and normalize the result to obtain the shooting direction. The stance lies behind the ball: move back by  distance  along that direction, then sideways by  lateral  to allow space for the kicking leg. This exercise defines its own offset convention; it does not replace calibrated entry values in the physical skill.  Open  plan.svg  to inspect the stance, ball, and goal.  plan.json  gives the target position and heading. Change distance from 0.18 to 0.25 with a new output directory; predict the direction of movement and check it. This command computes geometry from known points. It runs no physics and does not prove reachability.  The full task also handles yaw drift, delayed gait response, and targets leaving view at close range. Approach therefore updates observations and checks stopping conditions repeatedly. If valid range or floor support is lost, stop or retreat within constraints and observe again. Unknown space cannot be declared free space.    When should the robot look again?      A focused view of ball observation and head motion.   A first observation supplies an initial target, but motion changes relative geometry and estimation error accumulates. The current controller verifies position before kicking. Retreat is a recovery option, not a mandatory phase.   Check your understanding  Why not kick at the last known location when the ball leaves view?   Show explanation  Motion changes relative position and the estimate may be stale. Check time, pose and stance before kicking; reobserve when necessary.

title: Complete the autonomous task
text:
Run the fixed detector first      Eight actual fixed-detector outputs on separate images, with class labels and confidence scores. Click to enlarge. These examples do not estimate overall accuracy.     Terminal · Bash  Copy command    python3 scripts/workshop.py detect \
  --model models/indoor-detector/detector.pt \
  --source datasets/indoor-sample/images \
  --output outputs/detection-01    Expected result: images with ball and goal detections. Inspect small targets, image boundaries, and occlusion. Confidence is a model score, not a guarantee that a detection is correct.    1 RGB image   2 Detection box   3 Image ray   4 Range and ground constraints   5 Target in the body frame   This detector is adapted to the steel-mesh goal and marked mat. Eight illustrations from the held-out image split cover four patterns; the original detector and exercise dataset remain available. Bounding boxes still require post-base extraction and known-dimension localization before planning.    Practice training a detector    Terminal · Bash  Copy command    python3 scripts/workshop.py train-detector \
  --data datasets/sample/data.yaml \
  --epochs 5 \
  --batch 8 \
  --seed 303 \
  --output outputs/student-detector-01    The small dataset and five epochs introduce data, labels, training, and validation; this is not a full training recipe. Inspect loss curves and validation images. To improve quality, diversify scenes and keep training, validation, and test scenes separate.   Keep the course detector downstream  Chapters 6 and 7 use  models/detector.pt  by default. The practice model does not replace it. Detection mAP measures detection quality, not shooting success.     Inspect labels and detections  The sample has 40 images split into 24 training, 8 validation, and 8 test images. Class 0 is the ball and class 1 the goal. Each YOLO label row is  class cx cy width height , with the last four values normalized by image dimensions. A horizontal center of 0.5 means halfway across the image, not 0.5 meters in the world.  Choose one clear prediction and one difficult example. Check missed objects, false detections, and misplaced boxes, then compare object size and position. High confidence cannot repair camera calibration or turn a 2D box into depth. Navigation still requires range, attitude, timestamps, and validity checks.   Check your understanding  Can a ball label centered at (0.6, 0.4) be used directly as a navigation target at (0.6 m, 0.4 m)?   Show explanation  No. These are normalized image coordinates. A camera model and range or ground constraint are needed to obtain robot-relative position.      What must adapt when the scene changes?  Domain randomization exposes a model to meaningful variation during training. Apply it to the affected component: mat colours, markings, light and mesh affect RGB detection; friction, voltage, delay, mass and contacts affect locomotion and kicking. This system combines detection, geometry, Nav2 and action policies; it does not use a vision-language-action model such as GR00T.      Variation  Main effect  Response      Mat A–D, light, camera pose  Boxes and contours  Generate varied RGB data; split by scene    Goal size/location and ball diameter  Metric scale, map and scoring  Update geometry contracts, not only textures    Friction, voltage, delay and mass  Gait, impact and recovery  Measure ranges; test whether policy adaptation is needed    Unknown obstacles, edges or deformation  Traversability and contact  Extend sensing/physics and then test planning/control      The steel-mesh goal and marked mat changed detection: development images showed missed goals and field-line false positives with the original detector. Perception was therefore fine-tuned while the walking, kicking and residual weights were preserved. The dataset contains four mat patterns with lighting, position and camera variations: 48 scene seeds and 768 images. All patterns and views from one scene belong to one split to avoid leakage.  The detector was fine-tuned for 60 epochs using 512 training, 128 validation and 128 test images. Held-out mAP50 is 0.945 and mAP50–95 is 0.920. These measure detection quality, not autonomous task success or the isolated benefit of randomization; that requires a matched-data, matched-budget ablation. Localization, paths, kicks, goal crossing and recovery require separate task tests.  Let failures determine whether to widen randomization. Test one fixed model on all four mats, then on unseen lighting and ball positions. Lost ball contours near white lines point to perception; correct recognition and stance followed by slip or failed recovery point to dynamics. Avoid changing every parameter at once, which obscures the cause.  Check your understanding: can lighting randomization fix localization after widening the goal but keeping the old centre spacing and map? No. Converting pixels to metres depends on the actual dimensions; correct the geometry contract first.  This fine-tuning run used 60 epochs and about 4.3 minutes of training wall time, excluding collection, export and complete simulations. Appearance and light variation target perception. Changing known goal dimensions also requires matching localization priors, maps and scoring, or a separate method that estimates unknown dimensions.      Same 128 held-out indoor images  mAP50  mAP50–95      Original detector  0.273  0.199    Adapted detector  0.945  0.920      This comparison supports adapting the detector to the new scene. It compares old and adapted models, not training with versus without randomization, so it does not isolate a causal randomization benefit. Better detection still leaves observation freshness, path handoff and recovery to validate.    Check stance geometry first    Terminal  Copy command    python3 scripts/workshop.py plan \
  --ball 0.08 0.03 --goal 0.68 0 \
  --distance 0.18 --lateral 0.035 \
  --output outputs/stance-plan-01    Inspect plan.svg and compare with the previous chapter’s equation. This exercise checks geometry with supplied points; the full task obtains targets from sensors.    Understand a teacher and a residual  The course kick combines a fixed base policy with a trained residual model. The residual adjusts the base behavior, so observations, action scale, actuators, and timing must match. Removing one model does not leave an equivalent skill.    Terminal · Bash  Copy command    python3 scripts/workshop.py inspect-model --model models/kick-teacher.onnx
python3 scripts/workshop.py inspect-model --model models/kick-residual.onnx    Find both files in the model inventory. Compare their input and output shapes and distinguish robot-state inputs from task inputs. The complete task uses the pair in Chapter 7; retraining is not required here.    Understand the complete system  This is not a single network issuing a “score” command. A walking policy controls the body, a detector supplies visual targets, range and attitude constrain relative position, a state machine decides when to observe, walk, and kick, and the kick models execute contact and recovery.    1 RGB + ToF + IMU   2 Target estimates   3 Navigate and align   4 Fixed kick models   5 Task evaluation       One complete direct-shot example. The inset shows the actual robot camera synchronized with the full scene. One demonstration is not a success-rate estimate.     Run the complete teaching scene    Terminal · Bash  Copy command    python3 scripts/workshop.py football \
  --scene indoor --style A --record-hd \
  --seed 983102 \
  --seconds 180 \
  --output outputs/football-01    Expected result: an Isaac simulation window opens and one robot searches, approaches, aligns, and attempts a kick autonomously. The program uses the repository’s fixed models and saves video, traces, and results. The 180-second budget is simulation time, not wall-clock waiting time. Initialization and rendering can take longer.  This seed is a selected teaching fixture drawn from successful examples. It supports comparison on the same scene and is not a new independent success-rate sample. Do not manually move the robot or ball during execution. To stop, press Ctrl+C in the terminal and retain the logs.  The indoor fixture starts the robot at (−0.55, 0.04) m and ball at (0.02, 0) m, with the goal plane at x = 0.68 m. Robot and ball coordinates initialize the scene; goal position and dimensions are known map priors. Runtime robot and ball positions still come from sensor estimates. Select patterns with --style B, C or D, and change starts with --root-y or --ball-xy. Record altered conditions as separate tests.    Judge complete success    Terminal · Bash  Copy command    python3 scripts/workshop.py report --run outputs/football-01     A real foot–ball contact occurred.  The entire ball crossed the goal plane inside the opening.  The robot did not fall or exceed the specified mechanical bounds.  There was no premature ball contact, and the robot recovered after kicking.    Interpreting the reference result  The original simple field and narrower goal completed 9/10 independent tasks. That historical result does not transfer to the marked mat, steel-mesh goal and full-body contacts. The current A-pattern demonstration completed contact, whole-ball crossing and recovery in 17.485 task seconds, passing all 11 applicable checks. It is a development example, not an independent success-rate estimate. New pattern tests must remain separate.       Mat / independent seed  Complete task  Task time  Fall      A / 50001  Pass  13.565 s  No    B / 50002  Fail  11.260 s  No    C / 50003  Fail  180.000 s  No    D / 50004  Fail  4.225 s  No      Four predeclared new seeds at the same standard start, one per mat, completed 1/4 full tasks. Passing applicable record audits is distinct from task success. Pattern and seed vary together, so this does not isolate a pattern effect or estimate broad reliability. See the  new-scene trial records .  All three failures occurred before the kick: B estimated the ball outside the kick range, then could not satisfy the current-body guard during retreat recovery; its ball observation had also expired by the stop; C cycled through reacquisition and alignment until the 180-second limit; D stopped its fine approach because a fresh goal observation was unavailable. None fell. A new scene therefore needs more than refreshed media or a strong detection score. Inspect target-point localization, observation validity and planning handoff before choosing additional training data; these trials do not establish a failure of the walking or kicking policies.    Design a small evaluation  Write down seeds and success criteria before running. Record goals, falls, contact, and recovery for every episode. Do not replace a failure with a retry. A model or parameter change defines a separate experiment.    Terminal · Bash  Copy command    python3 scripts/workshop.py football \
  --seed 990001 \
  --seconds 180 \
  --output outputs/football-new-seed-01     Check your understanding  Why can the task fail even when detection mAP is high and the walking policy stays upright?   Show explanation  Success depends on interfaces between modules. Targets can leave view, coordinates or observation age can become unsuitable, and position or heading may fail the kick conditions. Module metrics do not replace end-to-end evaluation.      Locate a problem from a failed run  First check whether  result.json  was produced. If not, inspect the terminal error and installation or runtime conditions: that is an execution failure. If results exist, distinguish failure to find the ball, failure to reach a kicking stance, contact without a goal, and failure to recover after scoring. A normal process exit does not mean the robot completed the task.   course_evaluation.passed  combines physical scoring and applicable checks.  scorer  retains contact, goal crossing, and fall information. In synchronized views, inspect the stance before first contact and posture after kicking. A short clip of the ball crossing the line is insufficient for a full-task judgment.  The original simple-field combination completed 9/10 independent tasks. The new mat and steel goal change appearance, geometry and contacts, requiring separate evaluation. Default seed 983102 demonstrates the new scene; repetitions are not independent samples.

title: Recap and a harder football challenge
text: From skills to a complete task   Scroll horizontally to view the full diagram    Learning through eight chapters  Experience：Keyboard → robot structure；Train and transfer：Flat → slopes → skills；Act autonomously：Sensing → planning → goal       Learning through eight chapters     Experience  Keyboard → robot structure   Train and transfer  Flat → slopes → skills   Act autonomously  Sensing → planning → goal    Isaac Sim provides an observable, resettable world. Isaac Lab organizes experience collection, policy learning and evaluation into reproducible experiments.       Capability  What you have done      Use skills  Load official ONNX actors and issue keyboard commands    Understand the robot  Inspect joints, load paths, sensors and control timing    Train skills  Collect parallel experience, update PPO and export an actor    Test generalization  Compare flat ground and slopes under matched conditions    Complete a task  Connect perception, localization, planning, walking and kicking      A motion actor solves how to move. A complete system also decides what to do, where the target is, whether information is reliable and when to switch skills. Keep demonstrations, skill benchmarks and task-level evaluation distinct.    Challenge: slopes, uneven ground and obstacles  Suppose the pitch has slopes, uneven patches and obstacles. Can the robot still score? This is a design challenge only; it is not implemented in the course.      Change  Questions to investigate      Slopes  Can the actor balance? Does the ball roll before contact?    Uneven ground  Is projection onto z = 0 valid? Is local surface height or depth needed?    Obstacles  How can a map provide clearance and support replanning?    Inclined kick surface  Are the flat-ground starting pose, ball relation and recovery conditions still valid?    More complex task  How can perception, navigation and motion failures be separated?      Draft a one-page proposal: scene variables, sensors, reusable policies, new training needs, data splits, success criteria and compute budget. Use Isaac Sim for scenes and Isaac Lab for terrain and skill evaluation.    One final question   Check your understanding  Why do slope walking and flat-pitch shooting not establish slope-pitch autonomous shooting?   Show explanation  The combined task changes ball motion, localization assumptions and kicking conditions. It needs its own end-to-end evaluation.

title: Models and data
text: Course model inventory      File  Purpose       walk.onnx   Fixed walking policy     terrain-walk.onnx   Chapter4 fixed terrain walking actor, about0.79 MB     kick-teacher.onnx   Base kicking action     kick-residual.onnx   Residual kick adjustment     kick-checkpoint.pt   Retained kick training checkpoint     detector.pt   Fixed visual detector     detector.onnx   ONNX detector export     indoor-detector/detector.pt  /  indoor-detector/detector.onnx   Indoor steel-goal detector; new scene default        Terminal · Bash  Copy command    python3 scripts/workshop.py verify-models    These files are included in Git without Git LFS or a separate model account.  models/manifest.json  records sizes, sources, and SHA-256 identities. Model identity checks guard against accidental same-name replacements. The added detector has a separate models/indoor-detector/deployment.json with relative paths and hashes; the original seven files are unchanged.    Practice data and your outputs   datasets/sample/  is a small image-and-label practice set for detector inference and short training. It is not enough to establish real-world generalization. Student checkpoints and logs belong in  outputs/ ; do not copy them over the course files in  models/ .    Sources and usage terms  Robot geometry, community policies, and dependencies retain their source terms. The course-code license does not override third-party asset licenses. Before redistributing changes, read the repository’s  attribution and license notices .

title: Troubleshooting
text:
Start with the environment report    Terminal · Bash  Copy command    python3 scripts/workshop.py doctor
python3 scripts/workshop.py verify-models    The first failure is more useful than repeatedly launching a full training run. Check the repository directory, the selected runtime, and all model checks.    Common issues      Symptom  What to check      No GUI window  Use the GPU desktop terminal and check DISPLAY and the driver. A remote text shell is not a graphical desktop.    First launch is slow  Check for downloads and compilation. Allow initialization and avoid starting duplicate instances.    Output directory exists  Choose a new run name and preserve the previous result.    Out of memory  Reduce training environments or detector batch size. Avoid concurrent simulations.    Model hash mismatch  Restore the repository model and check for accidental overwrites.    Practice policy walks poorly  A short run teaches the workflow. Inspect reward, episode length, and evaluation. Continue with fixed models.    Robot stops or does not score  Inspect the task report and observation validity. Stopping can be appropriate when information is missing; it is not a goal.        Inspect a run    Terminal · Bash  Copy command    python3 scripts/workshop.py report --run outputs/football-01    When reporting an issue, include the command, seed, environment report, and first error. A success/failure label alone is not enough. Do not include passwords or access tokens.

title: Further learning and references
text: Robotics and simulation  Begin with task observations, actions, and rewards, then explore physics and sensors. Course commands target fixed versions; current documentation may describe newer versions. Check the version before applying changes.    Suggested extensions   Vary the Chapter 3 training budget and compare on the same unseen seeds.  Add backgrounds and lighting conditions to Chapter 5 and evaluate generalization.  Visualize Chapter 7 target positions and headings for different ball locations.  Predefine new seeds for Chapter 7 and retain all successes and failures.
